p: Lieutenant Marcellus Jones, commanding the vedette post of Company E, 8th Illinois Cavalry, borrowed Sergeant Levi Shafer's carbine. He rested the barrel on a fence rail along the Knoxlyn Ridge. In the distance, perhaps 700 yards away, a mounted Confederate officer rode along the pike ahead of his advancing column.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Shot”, paragraph 2 of 7

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Shot”, paragraph 3 of 7

p: The shot missed. The officer rode on. But the sound of that single shot rolled across the fields and into the histories of both nations.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Shot”, paragraph 4 of 7

p: It was approximately 7:30 in the morning. The Battle of Gettysburg had begun.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Shot”, paragraph 5 of 7

p: Jones had no way of knowing what his missed shot had set in motion. He could not know that 51,000 men would become casualties on this ground over the next three days. He could not know that the shot he had just fired — borrowed, aimed from a fence rail, and wasted — would be commemorated by a monument that still stands on Knoxlyn Ridge today.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Shot”, paragraph 6 of 7

p: He rode back to report what he had seen. Behind him, Heth's Confederate division continued its march toward Gettysburg.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “The First Shot”, paragraph 7 of 7

p: John Fulton Reynolds was, by nearly universal agreement, the best corps commander in the Army of the Potomac. Meade had offered him command of the entire army three days earlier. Reynolds had refused — he wanted the freedom to fight without political interference. He had ridden ahead of his corps to Gettysburg that morning to see the situation for himself.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: What he saw at the Seminary convinced him that the Union army had to fight here. He sent a courier galloping south: bring the I Corps forward at the double-quick. And then, because Reynolds was that kind of general, he did not wait at the Seminary. He rode forward to lead the attack himself.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The Iron Brigade — his beloved Iron Brigade — was double-quicking across the fields toward the dark woods of Herbst. Reynolds rode to their head. He waved them forward into the trees, shouting encouragement.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: It struck Reynolds behind the right ear. He fell from his saddle without a word. By the time his aides reached him, he was already dead.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: He was 42 years old. He had never married. He had been engaged to a woman named Kate Hewitt; her name was found on a ring he wore. She had been waiting for him.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The Iron Brigade went into Herbst Woods and broke Archer's Confederate brigade — the attack Reynolds had set in motion with his life. But Reynolds was gone, and the Army of the Potomac would fight the next two days without the man who might have made all the difference.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The Iron Brigade swept through Herbst Woods like a tide. Archer's Tennessee and Alabama brigade had advanced confidently that morning — they expected Pennsylvania militia, not the best infantry in the Army of the Potomac.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The black hats changed everything. A Confederate soldier who recognized them shouted a warning: 'That's no militia — that's the Army of the Potomac!' But it was too late.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: The Iron Brigade's left regiments — the 2nd and 7th Wisconsin — swept south of the Chambersburg Pike and curled around Archer's right flank. Archer's brigade, caught in the flank, broke. Men streamed back toward Willoughby Run, some plunging into the water to escape.
